sql_threads.py:147-153: the done-callback is attached only after submit() returns a future (line 153), so if submit raises (e.g. RuntimeError after shutdown) no callback exists and the direct slot.release() at line 150 is the only release; this runs on the event-loop coroutine, so a direct release is safe. On success, the callback releases once via _release_slot with call_soon_threadsafe (line 107-111). The caller never sees the future from a raising submit, so there is no double release. sql_threads.py:139-142 wraps slot.acquire() in asyncio.wait_for and catches builtin TimeoutError. On 3.11+ asyncio.TimeoutError is an alias of TimeoutError, so the catch is right. A cancelled Semaphore.acquire does not keep a decremented count (it is only decremented on successful acquire, and 3.11+ restores wakeups on cancel). wait_for on timeout cancels and awaits the inner task. If the acquire had already completed, wait_for returns its result instead of timing out (3.11), or the timeout context is not triggered (3.12). So SqlWorkersBusyError is raised only when no slot was acquired. Verified from knowledge of CPython behaviour; CPython source was not read here.

sql_threads.py:154-158 awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future) and on CancelledError adds _log_call_after_cancel. CPython's _chain_future propagates asyncio-side cancellation by calling source.cancel() on the concurrent future, but Future.cancel() on a RUNNING future returns False and leaves state unchanged. So for a still-running call, the task cancellation neither cancels nor marks it, and the done callback later sees the real result or exception (lines 114-123). Caveat: a future submitted but not yet picked up by a worker (PENDING) would be cancelled by this propagation. _log_call_after_cancel returns early on cancelled() (line 115), and the slot-release callback still fires, so this is benign. The claim is scoped to a running call, so I treat it as holding.

sql_threads.py:144-148: on the fast path Semaphore.acquire does not suspend, and nothing awaits between acquire and submit, so cancellation cannot land there. The slow path (line 140) uses asyncio.wait_for(slot.acquire(), ...). pyproject.toml:10 allows Python >=3.11. In 3.11, wait_for wraps acquire in a task, and on CancelledError it does 'if fut.done(): return fut.result()'. That swallows the cancellation. If a slot is granted in the same loop tick the waiter is cancelled, wait_for returns normally, line 146-148 submits, and the query runs although its caller was cancelled. At head, src/sqllens/agent/integrations/sql_threads.py has no custom worker loop or catch-all hand-back block. run_blocking_sql (lines 146-158) submits to a standard concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor (_get_executor, lines 84-91). The executor sets the future's result or exception itself, so the caller's wrap_future await cannot hang on a failed hand-back. A search of the file found no _DaemonThreadPool or except BaseException hand-back block. The only except BaseException is around submit (lines 149-151), and it releases the slot and re-raises.

Defect fixed at head: sql_threads.py:137-142 waits for a slot via asyncio.wait_for(slot.acquire(), WORKER_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S=60s) (line 62) and raises SqlWorkersBusyError (line 69-73, 'All database workers are busy; try again shortly.') on timeout. The ninth caller therefore gets a clear error rather than waiting without limit. The semaphore replaces the unbounded queue. Contract is documented in the module docstring lines 15-19.

Fixed at head. _DaemonThreadPool, _busy and qsize() no longer exist in sql_threads.py. Saturation is now decided by an asyncio.Semaphore: `if slot.locked(): _warn_saturated()` (line 137). The semaphore is acquired before executor submit (lines 140-148), so the executor queue cannot grow beyond the slot count unseen. Any call that finds all slots taken warns, and the rate limit is applied under _lock (lines 97-101). The message (lines 102-104) prints only the constant SQL_WORKER_THREADS, so there is no unlocked queue-length read. I searched the file for qsize and _busy and found no readers.
